summary: Children first recognise and name a few star patterns (Orion with its belt, the Plough/Big Dipper — a star pattern within the constellation Ursa Major — Leo, Cassiopeia), then explain why some are seasonal: at night we look OUTWARD, away from the Sun, into space, and as Earth travels around its orbit through the year 'away from the Sun' points at a different patch of stars each season. Seen from the Northern Hemisphere, a constellation like Orion is 'missing' in summer because it is then up in the DAYTIME sky, on the Sun's side, its faint light lost in daylight. Key moves: (1) recognition first, then (2) explain seasonal visibility by Earth's ORBIT, carefully distinguished from the daily SPIN, and contrasted with circumpolar stars near Polaris that stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes.
misconceptions: Attributing seasonal star changes to Earth's daily SPIN (day/night) rather than its yearly ORBIT — conflating the two motions.
Thinking the constellations themselves move away or change shape seasonally, rather than our night-time viewing direction changing as Earth orbits.
Believing a 'missing' constellation has disappeared or been destroyed, not realising it is in the daytime sky (on the Sun's side) and lost in sunlight.
Assuming ALL constellations are seasonal, missing that circumpolar ones (Plough, Cassiopeia) stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes.
Confusing the cause of seasonal star visibility with the cause of the seasons themselves (axial tilt) — they are different, orbit-related but distinct.
Thinking stars are joined by real lines or that a constellation is a single object rather than a pattern of stars at very different distances.

activities.title: Drag Earth round its orbit and watch tonight's sky change
steps: Study two linked views side by side: a bird's-eye (top-down) view of Earth orbiting the Sun, and the night sky a child on Earth would actually see at midnight.

Slowly move Earth around its year-long loop. On the orbit view the night side (facing away from the Sun) is shaded; watch the night-sky window swap in which named constellations are up in the night sky for each position.

Find Orion shining high in the southern midnight sky in (northern-hemisphere) winter; then move Earth toward summer and watch how, as Earth moves, the Sun comes to lie in Orion's direction as seen from Earth, so Orion ends up on Earth's day side and fades out of the night-sky window, with a label noting 'now up in the daytime — hidden by the Sun'.
Use a 'spin vs orbit' toggle: see that the daily spin only slides the SAME stars east-to-west across the night, while the yearly orbit changes WHICH constellations are there at all.
Notice that the Plough/Cassiopeia, near the pole (Polaris), stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes while Orion comes and goes.
activities.insight: The stars didn't go anywhere — WE moved around the Sun, so at night we face a different part of space. The yearly orbit (not the daily spin) changes which constellations are up at night, and a 'missing' summer constellation is really in the daytime sky on the Sun's side.

activities.title: Four-season orbit diagram with reveal cards
steps: Look at a labelled orbit diagram with the Sun at the centre and Earth at four seasonal positions.
Reveal, for each of the four positions, that season's constellations and a night-side arrow pointing outward into space.
Reveal a constellation to see its name and star-join pattern (Orion, Ursa Major with its Plough pattern, Leo, Cassiopeia).
Open the reveal on a summer-hidden Orion to read 'it's in the daytime sky now'.
Compare the four snapshots to notice which constellations change season-to-season and which (circumpolar) stay.
activities.insight: Across the four seasons, Earth's night side points outward in different directions, so different constellations are overhead — and the ones that lie toward the Sun in a given season are up in the daytime instead.

activities.title: Stand on Earth and advance the date (immersive view)
steps: Take a first-person 'look up from Earth' view of the night sky.
Advance the date forward through the months and watch which constellations are visible change.
Relate the immersive view back to the top-down orbit position so the ground-view change connects to Earth's movement around the Sun.
activities.insight: From the ground, the visible constellations change through the year; this is the same orbit effect seen from a different vantage, reinforcing that our changing position changes what we face at night.

activities.title: Check recognition and reasoning
steps: Match each constellation to its name (Orion, Ursa Major with its Plough pattern, Leo, Cassiopeia).
Answer: 'Why do we see different constellations in different seasons?' choosing the orbit explanation over the daily-spin distractor.

Sequence the seasonal constellations (e.g. Orion, Leo) by the season in which they are best seen in the evening sky, and note that circumpolar ones (Plough, Cassiopeia) are visible in every season from mid-northern latitudes.
Explain in your own words where Orion is during summer.
activities.insight: Consolidate naming and articulate the orbit-based reason, separating it from the daily-spin explanation.

checkQuestion: We can see the constellation Orion clearly on winter nights, but not on summer nights. Has Orion moved away or disappeared by summer — or is it still there somehow? Tell me WHY we can't see it in summer.
checkAnswer: Orion hasn't moved or gone anywhere — in summer it is still there, but it's up in the sky during the DAYTIME, on the same side as the Sun, so the Sun's glare drowns it out and we can't see it at night. As Earth travels around the Sun through the year, our night side faces different directions in space, so at night we look out at different constellations in different seasons. In winter our night side faces toward Orion; in summer our night side faces the opposite way, so Orion is only 'up' in the daytime.
